prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world the agent's observation shows the target shifted: the target, missing, extra and target-height channels are rolled 4 columns toward higher x, wrapping around. The world, its designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
The start network gave up straight away: every greedy episode is an immediate DONE, and the learning curve shrinks to length 1. The traces show why. The target heights the agent observes are the real design shifted 4 columns along x, wrapping round (X/2). Every row of both diagnostic designs matches this; it is not a mirror image. So the target sits in the wrong place compared with the build and the action grid. Small local convolutions cannot connect a cell to the cell 4 columns away, so placements look random, rewards are negative, and DONE (reward 0) wins. The missing/extra channels may be shifted too, since the agent learned nothing from them. The top priority is lining the target back up. This round tests: (1) a fixed shift back by X/2, (2) a general version that gives the first learned layer every x-shift and lets it pick, (3) the fixed shift plus a recipe that collects more samples and explores more, to resist the DONE collapse.

### Round 2
The observed target is the design shifted X/2 columns with wrap-around. Lining the target back up with the build fixed the collapse to DONE. With that fix, dev success was 0.59 on the default recipe and 0.63 with r1c3's recipe (ppo_epochs 2, which gives about 1.9x the samples). Seed spread is about ±0.14, so these two results are not clearly different. Learning a pick among all x-shifts also worked (0.44), so the method should carry over to other grid sizes. Training success was still rising at the end of every run, which suggests the agent is short of samples. In both diagnostic traces the agent fills the ground layer and layer 1 correctly, then chooses DONE while upper cells near rows 1–2, columns 1–2 are still missing. That points to two likely problems: the agent undervalues the +1 exact-build bonus, which gamma 0.95 discounts heavily, and its 5x5 receptive field is too small for upper layers and overhangs. Each training run took about 60 of the 900 seconds allowed, so time is not a constraint.

### Round 3
The observed target is shifted X/2 columns with wrap-around. Unrolling it fixed the instant-DONE collapse (0.59–0.63). Seed noise is large: r1c3's seeds scored 0.49 and 0.77, so gaps under about 0.15 mean little. ppo_epochs 1 (0.08) and gamma 0.99 (0.11) clearly hurt, even with similar gradient steps, so reusing data across epochs matters. The deeper trunk's collapse is confounded by its 1-epoch recipe. The traces show the agent filling layer 0 well, then saying DONE before placing upper or overhanging bricks (for example the 1x2 at layer 2 in design 1). Training success was still rising at the end, and there are only about 55 policy updates. Next: (1) twice as many smaller updates with the same samples per minibatch; (2) feed crisp per-cell stem features into the footprint head; (3) a new head that scores every possible landing layer z with shared weights and combines them with logsumexp.

### Round 4
Lining the shifted target up with the build was the key fix: the X/2 shift-back took dev success from 0 to about 0.6. Passing the per-cell stem features into the footprint head (r3c2) gave the best result, 0.70 (seeds 0.50 and 0.90), but that gain is within seed noise. Seed spread is very large. Moving the recipe away from ppo_epochs 2 with the default gamma did worse: 1 epoch, gamma 0.99 and 2x more updates all scored lower, and a deeper trunk collapsed to instant DONE. Training success was still rising at the end of every good run. In r3c2's trace the agent stops before placing one 1x2 overhang brick that needs exact per-cell landing reasoning, which pooled max/min/mean features lose. Two cheap levers remain: more gradient steps on the same samples (smaller minibatches add no counted compute), and a head that sees each footprint cell's features separately.

## Trial it ended with
name: r3c2 + 32 minibatches
hypothesis: Same network and recipe as r3c2, but n_minibatches goes from 16 to 32. This doubles the gradient steps per update (128 samples per minibatch) at no counted compute cost, so the number of training samples is unchanged. Learning was still rising at the end, so faster learning from the same data should raise dev success and help the slow seed. Refuted if 2-seed dev success falls below about 0.55.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).

reply.evidence: In Round 1 the scientist writes: "The target heights the agent observes are the real design shifted 4 columns along x, wrapping round (X/2)... it is not a mirror image." It adds that "the missing/extra channels may be shifted too." That covers what changed (the target channels in the observation) and how (a 4-column x-shift with wrap-around). It never says the shift goes toward higher x, and the other channels are only guessed at, but the core of the rule is stated.
